0.title: Reading the Last Things
0.essay:
The doctrine of the last things is among the most contested areas of Christian theology. Yet the disagreements take place within a framework every orthodox Christian shares, and it is worth stating that clearly first.

What all agree on

Every orthodox Christian believes that Jesus rose bodily from the dead, ascended in that body to the Father’s right hand, and will return bodily, visibly and gloriously at the end of history to judge the living and the dead. Every orthodox Christian believes history is moving towards a goal — the resurrection of the dead, the final judgment, a new creation — and that the goal is not in doubt, because it rests on the word of the God who raised Jesus. And every orthodox Christian believes the return of Christ will be sudden and transforming, “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye” (1 Corinthians 15:52).

What is disputed

What Christians disagree about is the sequence and shape of the events around that return: whether there is a literal thousand-year reign before or after it, whether the church will be taken out of the world before a period of great tribulation, whether Israel has a separate future programme distinct from the church, and how to read the highly symbolic language of Revelation.

The central text

The most disputed passage is Revelation 20, which describes Satan bound for “a thousand years,” and those who had died for Christ who “came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years” (Revelation 20:4). Does it describe a future earthly reign after Christ returns (premillennialism), the present reign of Christ between his two comings (amillennialism), or a coming golden age of gospel advance before his return (postmillennialism)? Much also turns on Matthew 24, Daniel 9, 1 Thessalonians 4, and how we read the Old Testament promises to Israel.

How we read

The biggest factor in which view someone holds is not which texts they read, but how they read them. Should Old Testament prophecy be read as literally as possible, or through the lens of its fulfilment in the New Testament? Dispensationalism insists on a consistently literal reading. Reformed covenant theology reads Old Testament prophecy as the apostles did, seeing its fulfilment in Christ in ways that often go beyond the letter.

Already and not yet

Every view must also wrestle with the New Testament’s tension between “already” and “not yet.” The kingdom has come: “the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew 12:28). Yet we still pray, “Your kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10). The resurrection has begun in Christ, “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20), yet the general resurrection is still to come. Satan has been decisively defeated, yet “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion” (1 Peter 5:8). How each view handles that tension largely shapes its structure.

A brief history

The early church held a variety of views. Justin Martyr and Irenaeus were premillennialists. Augustine, in The City of God, articulated what we now call amillennialism, and set the direction for the medieval and Reformation churches. Dispensationalism arose in the nineteenth century through John Nelson Darby and the Plymouth Brethren, and was spread by the Scofield Reference Bible (1909), and later by popular books and the Left Behind novels.

Why it matters

Eschatology shapes how we live now: our attitude to the world (is it to be renewed, or merely destroyed?), our engagement with culture, our understanding of Israel and the Middle East, our posture towards suffering (is tribulation to be escaped, or endured?), and our confidence that the gospel will triumph.

The chapters

This study presents the four main views fairly — Amillennialism, Historic Premillennialism, Dispensational Premillennialism and Postmillennialism — and ends with A Reformed Assessment.

For reflection

What have you been taught about the end times, and by whom? How has it shaped the way you live?

1.title: Amillennialism
1.essay:
Despite its name, amillennialism does not deny the millennium. It reads the “thousand years” of Revelation 20 symbolically, as the whole present age between Christ’s first and second comings.

The view in brief

In this age, Satan is bound in a specific sense, the gospel advances to all nations, and the souls of those who have died in Christ reign with him. The millennium is not a future event; it is the age in which we now live. Then Christ will return suddenly, the dead will be raised, the living transformed, the final judgment held, and the new heavens and new earth begun.

This has been the dominant view of the historic Reformed tradition, held by Augustine, Calvin, Louis Berkhof, Anthony Hoekema and most Reformed theologians today. It is not pessimistic. It does not expect the church to be overwhelmed. It is realistic: the church will see both gospel advance and growing opposition, fruit and tribulation, right up to the end.

Reading the Old Testament through the New

Amillennialism reads Old Testament prophecy through the New Testament, which repeatedly applies Israel’s promises to Christ and the church. The land becomes the new creation. The temple becomes Christ and his people. The nation becomes a people from every nation. There is no separate future programme for ethnic Israel; Israel’s promises are fulfilled in Christ and in all who are in him.

The binding of Satan

Revelation 20 says Satan was bound “so that he might not deceive the nations any longer, until the thousand years were ended” (Revelation 20:3). Amillennialists connect this with Christ’s victory at the cross. Jesus said, “Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out” (John 12:31). And: “how can someone enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? Then indeed he may plunder his house” (Matthew 12:29).

The binding is not the end of all Satan’s activity, but a specific restriction: he can no longer prevent the gospel from reaching the nations. In earlier ages God “allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways” (Acts 14:16). Now the gospel is going to every people.

But if Satan is bound, why does Peter call him a roaring lion, and Paul “the god of this world” (2 Corinthians 4:4)? Because the binding is specific in purpose, not total. A chained lion is still a lion. It can roar and do harm within the reach of its chain. The pictures address different aspects of his present activity.

The first resurrection

“Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! Over such the second death has no power” (Revelation 20:6). Premillennialists take this as a bodily resurrection before the millennium. Amillennialists, following the New Testament’s own use of resurrection language, see it as the spiritual resurrection of believers, who have “passed from death to life” (John 5:24). God has “raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:6). Others read it as the souls of the martyrs reigning with Christ in heaven.

Either way, its pastoral weight is great. The second death is the lake of fire (Revelation 20:14). Those who share in the first resurrection are safe from it. To a persecuted church, this says: you have already crossed the decisive threshold from death to life, and the final death cannot touch you. G. K. Beale’s commentary argues that the first resurrection is the “already” of salvation, and the bodily resurrection at Christ’s return its “not yet.”

One resurrection, one judgment

Jesus said, “Do not marvel at this, for an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:28–29). One hour, one coming out, distinguished only by its outcome. Paul spoke of “a resurrection of both the just and the unjust” (Acts 24:15).

Amillennialists see this as strong evidence against two resurrections separated by a thousand years. Premillennialists reply that “hour” can mean a longer period, and that Revelation 20 adds detail John 5 omits. But the plain sense of Jesus’ words is a single event. So the sequence is simple: Christ returns, the dead are raised, the living transformed, the final judgment held, and the eternal state begins. No secret rapture, no seven-year gap, no earthly millennium after the resurrection.

A world-affirming hope

Amillennialism is not an escape from earth to heaven. “But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells” (2 Peter 3:13). The new creation is this creation redeemed, renewed and glorified. Creation itself groans in hope of being set free (Romans 8:19–22). And when John says “the sea was no more” (Revelation 21:1), he uses the sea as Revelation’s symbol of chaos and the source of the beast (Revelation 13:1): everything opposed to God will be gone.

Amillennialism is sometimes dismissed as pessimistic or world-denying. That is a caricature. As Hoekema argued, if the new creation is this cosmos renewed rather than replaced, then culture-making matters. The present creation is not a disposable backdrop for saving souls. It is the raw material of the new heavens and earth.

The tradition

Augustine’s City of God set the terms of the debate for a thousand years, reading the millennium as the present age of the church. The Reformers followed him. Calvin dismissed millenarian speculation in his Institutes. The Reformed confessions do not address the millennium directly, but their framework fits the amillennial view. Geerhardus Vos’s The Pauline Eschatology and Hoekema’s The Bible and the Future are among its finest modern defences.

For reflection

What difference does it make to think of the present age as the time of Christ’s reign? How does the “first resurrection” comfort you?

2.title: Historic Premillennialism
2.essay:
Historic premillennialism holds that Christ will return before a literal thousand-year reign on earth. It has deep roots in the early church, and it deserves a careful hearing.

The view in brief

The return of Christ will be preceded by intensifying tribulation and apostasy. At his coming, the dead in Christ will be raised, Satan will be bound, and Christ will reign on earth with his resurrected saints for a thousand years. Then will come the resurrection of the wicked, the last judgment, and the eternal state. The sequence is: tribulation, Christ’s return, the millennium, the final judgment, the new creation.

It is called “historic” to distinguish it from the later dispensational form. Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Tertullian and Papias all held it. It does not depend on a distinction between Israel and the church, nor on a secret rapture. The church goes through the tribulation. Israel has no separate programme. Modern advocates include George Eldon Ladd and Wayne Grudem.

The dead in Christ will rise first

“For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first” (1 Thessalonians 4:16). The premillennialist reads “first” as meaning that this resurrection comes before another, the resurrection of the wicked, a thousand years later.

The amillennialist reads it differently: the dead in Christ rise first, and then the living are caught up with them (1 Thessalonians 4:17), a sequence within one event, not a gap of a thousand years. The question is real, but Paul’s purpose is plain in every reading: comfort. The dead in Christ are not lost. They will be raised, and we will be with them. “Therefore encourage one another with these words” (1 Thessalonians 4:18).

Two resurrections

Revelation 20 is the pivot of the debate. “They came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years. The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were ended. This is the first resurrection” (Revelation 20:4–5).

George Eldon Ladd argued that if “came to life” in verse 4 means bodily resurrection, the same words in verse 5 must mean the same kind of event: so there are two bodily resurrections, a thousand years apart. This is the strongest exegetical argument for premillennialism, and it carries weight even for those who finally prefer the amillennial reading.

He must reign until

Paul writes, “But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ. Then comes the end” (1 Corinthians 15:23–24). “For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25). Premillennialists see an interval here: Christ’s coming, then a reign, then the end.

Amillennialists answer that Christ is reigning now, at God’s right hand (Romans 8:34; Ephesians 1:20–22), and will reign until his enemies are subdued, which describes the present age, ending at his return. Paul goes on to say that “the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28), pointing to the eternal state rather than a millennium. The passage is genuinely contested.

The martyrs vindicated

One of the most powerful pastoral themes of Revelation 20 is the vindication of the martyrs: “I saw the souls of those who had been beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God” (Revelation 20:4). Those who lost their heads to Rome’s executioners will reign with Christ. Their humiliation is reversed. Whether read as bodily resurrection at Christ’s return, or as their present reign in heaven, the comfort is the same: their witness is eternally honoured. Richard Bauckham has shown that this vindication, more than chronology, is the main concern of Revelation 20.

How it differs from dispensationalism

Historic premillennialism shares with all orthodox views the conviction that Christ’s return will be visible and bodily: “This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11). But it differs from dispensationalism in four ways. There is no pre-tribulation rapture; the church endures the tribulation. There is no separate programme for ethnic Israel; Israel’s promises are fulfilled in Christ and the church. There is no rebuilt temple with restored sacrifices. And there is no rigid division between a “church age” and a “kingdom age.” That makes it far more compatible with covenant theology.

Its appeal

The early church’s premillennialism grew partly from persecution: the hope of a glorious earthly vindication of the martyrs was a comfort to those who suffered. Irenaeus, in Against Heresies, argued for a literal millennium as the completion of God’s purposes for the material creation. It was a simpler, more worshipful expectation than the later dispensational system.

Today it still appeals to many Reformed and evangelical Christians. It takes Christ’s visible, bodily return as the pivotal event. It reads Revelation 20 more literally than amillennialism, without dispensationalism’s elaborate system. And it gives a place for the vindication of the martyrs and the fulfilment of God’s purposes for the earth within history. Ladd’s The Presence of the Future remains its most influential modern treatment.

For reflection

Which arguments for historic premillennialism do you find strongest? What do you make of Ladd’s point about “came to life” in Revelation 20:4–5?

3.title: Dispensational Premillennialism
3.essay:
Dispensational premillennialism is the most widely held view of the end times in American evangelicalism. Those who hold it are taking Scripture seriously, and their convictions deserve a charitable hearing.

Serious and godly advocates

Dispensationalism has produced passionate missionary movements, earnest expectation of Christ’s return, and serious engagement with biblical prophecy. Christians who hold it — including John MacArthur, Chuck Swindoll, J. Vernon McGee and millions of ordinary believers — do so not because they read carelessly, but because it seems to them the most natural reading of Scripture’s prophetic texts.

The view in brief

Christ will return before a literal thousand-year reign on earth. Before that, the church will be caught up to meet him in a rapture, and there will be a seven-year tribulation during which God works dramatically among the nation of Israel. Then Christ will return with his saints, reign from Jerusalem for a thousand years, and fulfil God’s promises to Israel.

Two foundations

It rests on two commitments. First, reading prophecy with the same literalness as any other Scripture. If God promised Abraham a literal land, nation and descendants, those promises should be fulfilled literally. Second, the conviction that Israel and the church, though both loved by God, have distinct identities, roles and futures, and that merging them does violence to the specific promises of the Old Testament.

Its great strength is its regard for the integrity of prophecy. It refuses to let promises to Israel evaporate into vague spiritual fulfilment. When God promised David an eternal throne in Jerusalem, it insists, he meant a throne in Jerusalem. That is not wooden literalism but a serious commitment to God’s faithfulness to his word.

The rapture

“Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 4:17). The Latin Bible translated “caught up” with a word from which we get “rapture.” It describes a sudden, powerful seizure.

Dispensationalists note that believers meet the Lord “in the air,” and that the passage does not describe Christ completing his descent to earth. Together with Jesus’ promise — “I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also” (John 14:3) — this suggests to them a removal of the church before the tribulation. Whatever one concludes about the timing, the event itself — the bodily catching up of the saints to be with the Lord — is the shared hope of all evangelical views.

Not destined for wrath

“For God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 5:9). Dispensationalists see a pattern: God preserved Noah through the flood, rescued Lot before Sodom’s destruction, and kept Israel safe while the plagues fell on Egypt. They understand the tribulation of Revelation 6–19 as a time of divine wrath on a Christ-rejecting world, and read Christ’s promise to the church at Philadelphia — “I will keep you from the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world” (Revelation 3:10) — as exemption from it.

The comfort this offers is real, and should be honoured even by those who disagree. God does not pour out his wrath on his own children. The specific timing can be held with humility, while that conviction is held with confidence.

God has not rejected his people

“I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means!” (Romans 11:1). “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew” (Romans 11:2). Paul describes Israel’s stumbling as temporary and purposeful: “Now if their trespass means riches for the world, and if their failure means riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their full inclusion mean!” (Romans 11:12). And “even they, if they do not continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in” (Romans 11:23).

Dispensationalists read this as pointing to a future national turning of Israel to Christ. Israel and the Gentiles appear in Paul’s olive tree as distinct branches. That, they argue, is hard to explain without a continuing distinction.

The land

God told Abram, “To your offspring I give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates” (Genesis 15:18). Was that ever fully and permanently fulfilled? Perhaps partly under Solomon, but never completely. If God’s promises were literal when fulfilled in the past — Abraham did have a son; his descendants did go down to Egypt and enter Canaan — consistency suggests that unfulfilled parts await a literal future fulfilment. To spiritualise the land into “the new creation” feels to the dispensationalist like robbing Abraham of what God specifically promised. The concern for God’s faithfulness is genuine.

History and development

John Nelson Darby developed the system in the 1830s, wrestling with what he saw as the church’s failure to keep distinct the promises to Israel and to the church. The Scofield Reference Bible brought it to millions, and the Dallas Theological Seminary tradition — Chafer, Walvoord, Ryrie, Pentecost — developed it into a rigorous system.

Significant revision has since taken place within dispensationalism. “Progressive dispensationalism,” associated with Craig Blaising, Darrell Bock and Robert Saucy, recognises that the kingdom is already inaugurated in Christ’s present reign, and that the church is more continuous with Israel than earlier forms allowed. That shows dispensational scholars genuinely wrestling with the text.

Gifts to the church

Christians of other convictions can learn from dispensationalism: its passion for God’s promises to Israel, its expectation of Christ’s imminent return, and its missionary urgency. These are gifts to the whole church. The Dispensational Distinctives study explores this view in more detail.

For reflection

What do you find most compelling about dispensationalism’s concern for God’s faithfulness? Whatever the timing, how does 1 Thessalonians 4:17 encourage you?

4.title: Postmillennialism
4.essay:
Postmillennialism holds that Christ will return after a long era of gospel advance, in which the gospel progressively transforms the world and the nations are discipled. It is the most optimistic of the views.

The view in brief

The millennium is not necessarily a fixed thousand years, but an extended age of gospel triumph and Christian influence, at the end of which Christ returns to judge and to bring in the eternal state. Postmillennialists expect the Great Commission to be substantially accomplished, evil restrained, righteousness advanced, and Christ’s reign widely acknowledged before his return. “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ” (Revelation 11:15), in a real historical sense, before the end.

A Reformed pedigree

Postmillennialism has a distinguished Reformed history. Jonathan Edwards held a form of it, as did Charles Hodge, B. B. Warfield and Loraine Boettner. It fuelled the great missionary movements of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. William Carey’s call — “Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God” — sprang from confidence that the gospel would prevail worldwide. It has revived more recently, through writers such as Keith Mathison. It tends to produce a strongly culture-engaging Christianity.

All nations shall serve him

Postmillennialists find their strongest support not in Revelation but in the Psalms and the prophets. Psalm 72 prays for the king: “May all kings fall down before him, all nations serve him!” (Psalm 72:11). “May people be blessed in him, all nations call him blessed!” (Psalm 72:17). Written for Solomon, it points beyond him to the Messiah. The postmillennialist reads it as a promise to be fulfilled in history, before Christ returns.

The amillennialist does not dispute the promise, only its timing and mode. All nations will be blessed in him, through the gospel gathering a people from every nation (Revelation 7:9), and finally in the new creation. The psalm proclaims the certainty of the King’s universal rule, and on that all agree.

Until I make your enemies your footstool

“The LORD says to my Lord: ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool’” (Psalm 110:1). Postmillennialists see a present, progressive conquest: Christ is reigning now, and his enemies are being subdued through the gospel. And the Great Commission rests on his words, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18). The one with all authority has commanded the discipling of the nations. Surely, they argue, it will be substantially accomplished.

The mustard seed and the leaven

Jesus said the kingdom is like a mustard seed which, though the smallest of seeds, “becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches” (Matthew 13:32). The image echoes the language of universal empire in Daniel 4 and Ezekiel 17. And the kingdom is like leaven “that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, till it was all leavened” (Matthew 13:33). Postmillennialists read these as promises that the gospel will permeate and transform human society within history.

Other views see the same growth, but read it as the kingdom reaching all nations, rather than necessarily dominating every area of culture. All affirm that unexpected greatness will come from small beginnings.

The earth full of the knowledge of the LORD

Isaiah 11 describes the reign of the shoot of Jesse, under whom the wolf dwells with the lamb, and promises, “They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea” (Isaiah 11:9). Postmillennialists argue from its earthly, historical imagery that this describes history, not only eternity. Others note that Isaiah’s visions of the earth often include what we would call the new creation.

A golden age?

Unlike amillennialism, postmillennialism expects a real improvement in the state of the world before Christ returns: a golden age of faith, justice and culture, not merely the present mixture of advance and resistance continuing to the end.

Jonathan Edwards expected such an age of gospel expansion, and his History of the Work of Redemption presents world history as the progressive triumph of the gospel. B. B. Warfield held that the gospel, applied by the Spirit, was equal to the task of transforming the world.

The challenge of history

Two world wars, the Holocaust, persistent global suffering, and the decline of Christianity in the West have made postmillennialism seem less credible to many. The confident optimism of the nineteenth century is hard to sustain. Postmillennialists answer that the gospel’s advance is measured in centuries, not decades, and that over two thousand years — with the gospel now present in almost every nation on earth — the picture is far more encouraging than any one century’s setbacks suggest. The question is one of horizon, and of how we weigh Scripture’s promises against present experience.

For reflection

What can every Christian learn from postmillennialism’s confidence in the gospel? Where do you need to “expect great things from God”?

5.title: A Reformed Assessment
5.essay:
Having presented the four views as fairly as possible, we can now weigh them: with charity towards those who differ, clarity about what matters most, and confidence in what Scripture says plainly.

United in the blessed hope

Christians across all four positions love the same Lord, submit to the same Scripture and long for the same blessed hope: the personal, visible, glorious return of Jesus Christ. That shared conviction matters more than any millennial disagreement. A congregation containing amillennialists, premillennialists of both kinds and postmillennialists is united by the things that matter most, and divided only over the secondary interpretation of difficult prophetic texts. That is a reason for humble, mutually enriching conversation, not division.

What all four share

All four views affirm the visible, bodily, glorious return of Jesus Christ; the bodily resurrection of the dead, righteous and wicked; the final judgment of all people; the eternal state, with new creation for the redeemed and eternal separation for the unrepentant; the complete trustworthiness of every promise God has made; and the urgency of the gospel mission before the end. These are the load-bearing walls of Christian hope.

Every eye will see him

“Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him. Even so. Amen” (Revelation 1:7). This is the one certainty every view affirms without reservation. The return of Christ will be visible, universal and public, not a secret departure or a quiet spiritual presence. The verse combines Daniel’s glorious Son of Man coming with the clouds, and Zechariah’s pierced one. And John’s “Even so. Amen” is not resignation but longing: it is right that the King should come and every wrong be put right.

Where the Reformed tradition comes down

The Reformed tradition has historically favoured amillennialism: reading Revelation 20 as the present gospel age, understanding the church as the fulfilment of Israel’s promises in Christ, and expecting one general resurrection and judgment at Christ’s return. It has also welcomed historic premillennialism and postmillennialism as live options within the Reformed family.

Where it has been most consistently cautious is over the dispensational separation of Israel and the church as two peoples with two destinies. Not because concern for Israel is wrong — it is right and biblical — but because the New Testament presents the church as one new humanity in Christ. Christ “has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility” (Ephesians 2:14), “that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace” (Ephesians 2:15).

All Israel will be saved

Romans 11 is where the traditions most sharply divide. Paul calls it a mystery: “a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. And in this way all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25–26). Whatever he means, it is more than the present remnant.

Some in the covenant tradition read “all Israel” as the whole number of the elect, Jews and Gentiles together, “the Israel of God” (Galatians 6:16). Others read it as a future large-scale turning of Jewish people to Christ, not as a separate national programme, but as a remarkable work of the Spirit gathering them into the one people of God. The second is the better reading of Paul’s argument.

And all traditions should share Paul’s own response: wonder — “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11:33); humility, refusing any arrogance towards the Jewish people (Romans 11:18–20); and prayer — “Brothers, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved” (Romans 10:1).

The question of reading

The deepest disagreement is about how to read Old Testament prophecy. The dispensational instinct to read it as literally as possible flows from real reverence for Scripture and concern for God’s faithfulness. The covenant instinct to read it through its New Testament fulfilment flows from the conviction that the apostles themselves read it that way, applying Old Testament texts to Christ and the church in ways that go beyond the letter. Neither is careless, and both deserve serious engagement.

A verdict

Weighing the texts, the amillennial reading is the most faithful. Revelation is a book of symbols, and its “thousand years” fits the present reign of Christ from heaven. Jesus and Paul speak of one return, one resurrection of the just and the unjust, and one judgment (John 5:28–29; Acts 24:15; 2 Thessalonians 1:6–10). The New Testament nowhere teaches a secret rapture before a seven-year tribulation. This is held with charity: premillennial brothers and sisters share the same blessed hope.

What the tradition has learned

It would be ungenerous to engage dispensationalism only critically. Its passion for Old Testament prophecy has kept the church from lazily spiritualising the Hebrew Scriptures into mere moral illustrations. Its insistence on the specificity of God’s promises has pushed covenant theologians to explain more carefully what “fulfilment” means. Its concern for the Jewish people has been a valuable corrective to the antisemitism that has periodically stained the church’s history. And its expectation of an imminent return has fuelled missionary urgency.

What sort of people?

Scoffers in Peter’s day asked, “Where is the promise of his coming?” (2 Peter 3:4). Peter answered that God’s patience is not delay but mercy: “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). And the day will come suddenly, “like a thief” (2 Peter 3:10).

His practical question is the same for every view: “what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God” (2 Peter 3:11–12). The New Testament’s teaching on the last things always aims not at speculative timetables but at present faithfulness.

Holding the debate with grace

A wise pastor will preach the certainties — return, resurrection, judgment, new creation — with confidence and warmth. He will handle the disputed questions honestly, presenting the best arguments for each side rather than caricatures. He will model humility, since the greatest scholars of every age have not reached consensus. And he will unite the congregation around the prayer that transcends every system.

Maranatha

Paul preserved one of the church’s oldest prayers in Aramaic: “Our Lord, come!” (1 Corinthians 16:22). The New Testament closes with it: “Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20). The dispensationalist, the premillennialist, the amillennialist and the postmillennialist all pray it, to the same Lord, longing for the same day. They differ over the shape of the path. The destination, and the One they wait for, are the same. On the day he comes, every difference of interpretation will be resolved, and every eye will see what every believing heart has hoped for.

For reflection

Which certainties about Christ’s return most shape your life? How can you hold your own convictions about the end times firmly, and with charity towards those who differ?
